title: Al-Wahhab, the Bestower
hook: the Bestower, who gives without asking a return
tomorrow: Dadi says count what's been provided. where do you even start?

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-Qahhar: Yusuf naming the One over whom nothing prevails, from inside a prison. Nothing prevails over him. Today, a gift with no strings.
screen: `NOTHING PREVAILS OVER HIM.` → `A GIFT WITH NO STRINGS.`

segments.voice: A gift can come with a gift receipt tucked inside, or with an invisible one: you'll owe me. Yesterday's question was about the other kind. Jordan's grandmother, Miss Loretta, brought over the paint left from repainting her church hall, and wouldn't take a dollar for it. Why give like that? One question for today, then: what does a gift that asks nothing back look like?
screen: `THE INVISIBLE RECEIPT.` → `PAINT, AND NO PRICE.` → `A GIFT THAT ASKS NOTHING BACK?`

segments.voice: Islam's answer starts with a name: al-Wahhab, the Bestower, who gives without asking a return. The Qur'an puts it inside a prayer believers say, asking that their hearts not stray and for mercy from His presence, ending: "Lo! Thou, only Thou, art the Bestower." Only Thou. A human gift usually carries a hope: thanks, a favor later, at least being liked. Al-Wahhab needs nothing from anyone. And the Qur'an describes people who try to give in that same spirit, feeding the hungry and saying: "We wish for no reward nor thanks from you." Now the neighbor. Miss Loretta's church reads the same idea in its own book. In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus sends his followers out to heal, and tells them, in the King James words: "freely ye have received, freely give." Here's what the two share: a gift passes on easily when the giver remembers it was first given to them. The paint came from somewhere before it came to Amira's wall. And here's an honest difference. Christians hear Jesus's line inside their faith in him, whom they call the Son of God. In Islam, Jesus is honored as a prophet, and al-Wahhab is a name for God alone, the Giver behind every giver, with no one standing in between. Two houses, two ways of telling it, one thing worth saying to a friend tonight: the freest gifts come from people who know they've been given to.
screen: `AL-WAHHAB: GIVES, ASKS NOTHING BACK.` · `NO REWARD NOR THANKS FROM YOU.` · `MATTHEW: FREELY YE HAVE RECEIVED.` · `SHARED, AND HONESTLY DIFFERENT.` · then, large: `FREELY GIVEN.`

segments.voice: Choose one small thing you could give today with no way to be paid back: a snack left on a coworker's desk, a bill in a donation box, a compliment with your name left off. Hold it in mind through the sit, and each time a little you'll-owe-me slips in, let it go.
screen: `ONE GIFT, NO RECEIPT.` · `LET THE YOU'LL-OWE-ME GO.`

segments.voice: Al-Wahhab: the Bestower, who gives freely and asks no return. In the Qur'an's prayer: only Thou art the Bestower.
Worth keeping: freely given, freely passed on, no receipt inside. That's six names this week.

fork.setup: a neighbor fixes your bike and waves off any payment. you feel weird owing her. what fits today's lesson?
options: thank her warmly, and pass a free gift on to someone else.
insist on paying, so nobody owes anybody anything at all.
say nothing, since thanking her would turn it into a trade.
fork.reveal: thanks doesn't cancel a gift. passing it on is what both Matthew's line and the Bestower's name point toward.

chat.says: Miss Loretta won't take money for the paint. i baked her bread anyway. did i ruin the gift?
options: Not ruined. Thanks is fine; just don't turn her gift into a trade she never asked for.
Yes. A real gift can't be thanked at all; anything back cancels it out completely.
No, because now you're even, and being even is the whole point of a good gift.
chat.meaning: Al-Wahhab gives and asks nothing back; Matthew's line says pass it on. Bread as thanks is warm. Bread as payment would miss the point.
